newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Vietnam official says foreign aid misused.
newsitem.headline: Vietnam official says foreign aid misused.

text.p: Foreign aid to Vietnam, one of the world's poorest countries, is being abused or misused with fees for foreign advisers accounting for as much as 70 percent of costs in some projects, a government official has warned.

Only 20-30 percent of non-refundable aid was actually benefiting those it was targetting, Pham Cong Minh of the Committee for Management and Reception of Foreign Aid said in a critical indictment of loose aid management.
Minh said his committee had received some $770 million from foreign governments, international organisations and non-government organisations between 1991 and 1996.

In an article published in Tuesday's Thoi Bao Kinh Te Viet Nam newspaper, he said the money had been passed to government ministries who in turn distributed it to local recipients who were required to oversee its use through local management committees.
But problems had been found in all areas of management, distribution and relations with financial donors resulting in what he described as "uneven and unreasonable" distribution.
"Meanwhile many recipients have also considered non-repayable aid as 'money from God,' so that they take advantage of it to buy cars and equipment," he said.
Minh's most critical comments were reserved for projects involving the upgrade of technical equipment and the use of foreign advisers.

"In these projects, payment for foreign experts and advisers accounted for up to 70 percent of the total money," he said, adding that in one project to develop Vietnam's legal code foreign advisers had been paid between $10,000 and $18,000 per month.

Vietnam's per capita earnings stand at around $300 per year, making it one of the world's poorest countries. It has acquired a reputation as a darling of the international aid community since economic reforms were launched in the late 1980s.
Minh said donors were concerned their money might be misused and added that efforts were needed to ensure better management and accountability.
